Mission 1

Mission 1: France's Constitution calls regional languages heritage. Why can't state schools teach mostly in them?

Make a guess: France's Constitution calls regional languages heritage. Why can't state schools teach mostly in them?

Mission 1

What counts as le patrimoine?

  • Le patrimoine – heritage: what a community receives from the past and wants to pass on.
  • Three levels:
  • national: Versailles, Notre-Dame de Paris, the Mont-Saint-Michel;
  • regional: Breton or Basque culture, Alsatian timber-framed houses, the megaliths of Carnac;
  • local: a village church, a market, a mill, a local festival.
  • Two kinds:
  • material (matériel): buildings, sites, objects;
  • intangible (immatériel): know-how, traditions, languages, cuisine.
  • France has 56 sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List. Newest: Carnac (2025); the Normandy landing beaches and the royal fortresses of Languedoc (July 2026).
  • un monument historique – a listed building · transmettre – to pass on · un savoir-faire – know-how
Mission 1

Heritage reflects a culture

  • Notre-Dame de Paris: fire on 15 April 2019; restored and reopened in December 2024. Its rebuilding showed how much a monument can mean to a nation.
  • Intangible heritage (UNESCO): le repas gastronomique des Français (2010); the craft and culture of the baguette (2022).
  • Carnac (Brittany): thousands of standing stones, listed in 2025.
  • In the French-speaking world:
  • Île de Gorée (Senegal, listed 1978): a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
  • Old Québec (listed 1985): the historic French-speaking city centre.
  • Heritage can celebrate a culture, or remind it of a painful past.
  • une cathédrale · la reconstruction · un lieu de mémoire – a place of remembrance
Quick check
?Which of these is on UNESCO's list of France's intangible heritage (le patrimoine immatériel)?
Mission 1

Who protects heritage?

  • The state: the Ministry of Culture lists and protects monuments historiques.
  • Les Journées européennes du patrimoine (since 1984, every September): thousands of buildings, usually closed, open to the public.
  • Le Loto du patrimoine (since 2018): a lottery that funds the restoration of threatened local monuments.
  • Volunteers and associations: restoring churches, castles, mills.
  • Museums: from the Louvre to small local musées, they keep and explain the past.
  • restaurer – to restore · entretenir – to maintain, look after · un(e) bénévole – a volunteer · menacé(e) – under threat
Mission 1

Heritage and tourism

  • France had about 102 million international visitors in 2025, a record. It is the world's most visited country.
  • Benefits: jobs, money for upkeep, pride, a reason to keep traditions alive.
  • Problems: le surtourisme – overtourism: crowds, damage, rising rents, locals feeling pushed out.
  • Some sites now limit visitor numbers or require booking in high season.
  • un(e) touriste · attirer – to attract · rapporter de l'argent – to bring in money · un site classé – a protected site · préserver – to preserve
  • Your turn: "Tourism brings in money but threatens fragile sites."
    Show answer

    Le tourisme rapporte de l'argent mais menace les sites fragiles.

Quick check
?Grâce au tourisme, de nombreux monuments peuvent être entretenus. What does this mean?
Mission 1

Regional languages

  • In mainland France: Breton, Basque, Catalan, Corsican, Occitan, Alsatian, Flemish, Franco-Provençal.
  • Overseas: Creoles (Caribbean, Guiana, Réunion), Kanak languages, Tahitian.
  • 1539: the ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts makes French the language of law and administration.
  • Late 19th century: free compulsory schooling in French only; in many schools pupils were punished for speaking their regional language.
  • 1999: France signed the European charter on regional languages but has never ratified it.
  • 2008: the Constitution (article 75-1): « Les langues régionales appartiennent au patrimoine de la France. »
  • But article 2: « La langue de la République est le français. »
  • un locuteur / une locutrice – a speaker · une langue minoritaire · bilingue · transmettre une langue
Mission 1

The 2021 law and the immersion debate

  • L'enseignement immersif – immersion teaching: most lessons and school life in the regional language.
  • Associative schools such as Diwan (Breton, since 1977) teach this way.
  • 2021, loi Molac: a law to protect and promote regional languages.
  • The Conseil constitutionnel (21 May 2021) struck out two articles, citing article 2:
  • immersion teaching in state schools;
  • regional spelling marks in civil records, e.g. the ñ in the Breton first name Fañch.
  • Still in force: towns must help fund regional-language schools that pupils attend outside their town.
  • So: regional languages can be taught, and bilingual classes exist, but state schools cannot teach mainly in them.
Mission 1

Argue both sides

  • Should regional languages get a bigger place?
  • Yes (arguments supporters make):
  • Une langue qui disparaît, c'est une culture qui disparaît. – When a language dies, a culture dies.
  • L'immersion est le meilleur moyen de former de nouveaux locuteurs. – Immersion is the best way to create new speakers.
  • No, or with limits (arguments supporters make):
  • Le français est le ciment de l'unité nationale. – French holds the nation together.
  • Les élèves doivent d'abord maîtriser le français. – Pupils must master French first.
  • Linkers: Pour les défenseurs des langues régionales, … · Leurs opposants craignent que + subjunctive · Reste à savoir si …
  • Your turn: "Some fear that French may lose its place."
    Show answer

    Certains craignent que le français perde sa place.

Quick check
?Choose the correct French for: "Regional languages are taught in some schools."
Mission 1

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • le patrimoine (matériel / immatériel) · un monument historique · restaurer · entretenir · transmettre · un savoir-faire · le surtourisme · une langue régionale · un locuteur / une locutrice · bilingue · l'enseignement immersif · menacé(e)
  • Le patrimoine ne se limite pas aux monuments : il comprend aussi des savoir-faire et des langues.
  • Chaque année, de nombreux petits monuments sont restaurés grâce au Loto du patrimoine. (present passive)
  • Si l'on ne transmet pas les langues régionales aux enfants, elles risquent de disparaître. (si + present → present)
  • Component 1 card (5 min preparation, 5–6 min): Regional culture and heritage; historical sites and museums.
Mission check

?Which statement is accurate?

Heritage answers score when they move between levels (national, regional, local) and weigh benefits against costs with precise examples.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Why must French radio stations play a set share of songs in French, and does it still matter?

Make a guess: Why must French radio stations play a set share of songs in French, and does it still matter?

Mission 2

One language, many musics

  • La musique francophone: music in French, or by artists from French-speaking countries and communities.
  • France: chanson, rap, electronic music (la French touch).
  • Belgium: Stromae, Angèle. Québec: Céline Dion.
  • Caribbean: zouk (Kassav', from Guadeloupe and Martinique).
  • West and Central Africa: mbalax (Youssou N'Dour, Senegal), zouglou and coupé-décalé (Côte d'Ivoire), Congolese rumba, on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2021.
  • Many artists mix French with other languages: Wolof, Lingala, Creole, Arabic, English.
  • un genre musical · un(e) artiste · un tube – a hit · mêler – to mix
Mission 2

Changes and developments

  • 1940s–60s: la chanson à texte: the words matter most (Édith Piaf, Georges Brassens, Jacques Brel).
  • 1960s: les yé-yé: pop for teenagers, inspired by British and American rock (Johnny Hallyday, Françoise Hardy).
  • 1980s–90s: rap arrives and grows fast (MC Solaar, IAM, NTM).
  • Late 1990s: la French touch: French electronic music known worldwide (Daft Punk, Air).
  • 2010s–today: streaming; rap becomes the dominant genre; more women at the top (Aya Nakamura, Angèle).
  • évoluer – to evolve · s'inspirer de – to draw on · un courant – a movement
Quick check
?Which statement about francophone music is accurate?
Mission 2

Who listens, and how?

  • France's recorded music market: €1.07 billion in 2025, growing for ten years (SNEP).
  • Streaming is now the main way to listen: about 165 billion streams in 2025.
  • Vinyl is back: almost 6 million records sold in 2025.
  • French music is strong at home: 16 of the 20 best-selling albums of 2025 were French productions.
  • Young listeners: mainly streaming and short videos. Older listeners: more radio and CDs.
  • écouter en streaming · un abonnement – a subscription · télécharger – to download · un auditeur / une auditrice – a listener · le vinyle
Mission 2

Music's impact on popular culture

  • Language: rap spreads new words and expressions into everyday speech.
  • Fashion and image: streetwear, music videos (les clips), artists as brands.
  • National moments: at the Paris 2024 Olympic opening ceremony, Aya Nakamura (born in Mali) performed with the band of the Garde républicaine, and Céline Dion sang Édith Piaf's L'Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower.
  • La Fête de la musique (21 June, since 1982): free concerts in the streets, now copied in many countries.
  • Debates: who represents France? Should a national event reflect today's popular music?
  • un chanteur / une chanteuse · se produire – to perform · rassembler – to bring together
Quick check
?Les radios doivent diffuser au moins 40 % de chansons d'expression française. What does this mean?
Mission 2

How to safeguard francophone music

  • Radio quotas (law of 1994, in force 1996): music radio must play at least 40% French-language songs, half of them by new talents or new releases.
  • Quotas apply to radio, not to streaming platforms.
  • Le Centre national de la musique (CNM, 2020): public body that supports artists, venues and producers.
  • Festivals and prizes: Les Francofolies (La Rochelle, since 1985), les Victoires de la musique (since 1985).
  • Schools and local venues: music education, salles de concert, the Fête de la musique.
  • sauvegarder – to safeguard · soutenir – to support · diffuser – to broadcast · un quota
  • Your turn: "Without quotas, radio stations would play fewer French songs."
    Show answer

    Sans quotas, les radios diffuseraient moins de chansons françaises.

Mission 2

Argue both sides

  • Are radio quotas still useful?
  • Yes (arguments supporters make):
  • Les quotas aident les jeunes artistes à se faire connaître. – Quotas help young artists get known.
  • Sans eux, les radios passeraient surtout des tubes anglo-saxons. – Without them, radio would mostly play English-language hits.
  • No (arguments supporters make):
  • À l'ère du streaming, les quotas ont perdu leur sens. – In the streaming age, quotas have lost their point.
  • Imposer une langue limite la liberté artistique. – Imposing a language limits artistic freedom.
  • And English? Some French artists sing in English to reach the world (Daft Punk); others say French is part of their identity.
  • Linkers: Certes …, mais … · Il n'en reste pas moins que … · Selon ses défenseurs, …
Quick check
?Complete: « C'est une chanteuse ___ tout le monde parle. »
Mission 2

Talking about a song without quoting it

  • In exams, describe and analyse in your own words.
  • Dans cette chanson, l'artiste évoque … – In this song, the artist evokes …
  • Les paroles dénoncent / célèbrent … – The lyrics criticise / celebrate …
  • Le refrain répète une idée, ce qui souligne … – The chorus repeats an idea, which highlights …
  • Le rythme est lent / rapide ; la mélodie est … · Le clip montre … – The video shows …
  • les paroles (f pl) – lyrics · un couplet – a verse · le refrain – the chorus · rendre hommage à – to pay tribute to
  • Watch out: les paroles is plural: les paroles sont touchantes. Une parole alone means a word or a promise.
Mission 2

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • un genre musical · un tube · la chanson à texte · le rap · le streaming · un auditeur / une auditrice · diffuser · un quota · sauvegarder · se produire · les paroles · le refrain
  • C'est une artiste dont les chansons mêlent le français, l'argot et des mots d'autres langues. (dont)
  • Bien que le streaming domine, le vinyle connaît un retour en force. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • Si les radios n'étaient pas obligées de diffuser des chansons en français, les jeunes talents auraient plus de mal à percer. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • Component 1 card (5 min preparation, 5–6 min): Media, art, film and music; music in the lives of young people.
Mission check

?Which statement is accurate?

Name artists and countries, give one date and one figure, and weigh the quotas. That turns a music answer into an argument.

Mission 3

Mission 3: The first paid film screening was in Paris in 1895. Why do the French call cinema the seventh art?

Make a guess: The first paid film screening was in Paris in 1895. Why do the French call cinema the seventh art?

Mission 3

Why "the seventh art"?

  • 28 December 1895: the Lumière brothers hold the first public, paid film screening, in a room of the Grand Café in Paris.
  • In the 1910s–20s the critic Ricciotto Canudo (an Italian living in Paris) argued that cinema was a full art form.
  • His list: architecture, sculpture, painting, music, dance, poetry, then cinema, the seventh, because it combines them all (space, image, movement, sound, story).
  • Le septième art has been a common French name for cinema ever since.
  • un film · un long-métrage – a feature film · un court-métrage – a short film · le grand écran – the big screen
  • Watch out: un réalisateur / une réalisatrice = a film director. Un directeur runs a company or a school.
Mission 3

Evolution: the main stages

  • 1902: Georges Méliès, Le Voyage dans la Lune: special effects and fantasy.
  • 1930s: poetic realism and Jean Renoir (La Grande Illusion, 1937).
  • 1946: creation of the CNC (state film body) and the first Cannes festival.
  • 1959–60s: la Nouvelle Vague.
  • 1976: the first César awards, France's film prizes.
  • 2000s–2010s: huge popular comedies: Bienvenue chez les Ch'tis (2008) and Intouchables (2011) each sold close to 20 million tickets.
  • 2023: Justine Triet's Anatomie d'une chute wins the Palme d'or (then an Oscar for its screenplay in 2024).
  • Today: streaming platforms alongside cinemas.
Quick check
?Which of these came first?
Mission 3

La Nouvelle Vague

  • Late 1950s–1960s: young critics from the magazine Les Cahiers du cinéma start making films.
  • Key films: Les Quatre Cents Coups (François Truffaut, 1959) · À bout de souffle (Jean-Luc Godard, 1960) · Cléo de 5 à 7 (Agnès Varda, 1962).
  • What was new:
  • filming outdoors, in real streets, with natural light;
  • light, hand-held cameras and small budgets;
  • young, unknown actors;
  • jump cuts and breaking the rules of continuity;
  • the director as auteur: the film expresses one person's vision.
  • le tournage – filming, the shoot · tourner un film – to shoot a film · un(e) cinéaste – a film-maker · une caméra – a film camera
Mission 3

A national passion?

  • France is Europe's largest cinema market (CNC).
  • 2024: 181.5 million tickets sold; French films took 44.7% of them.
  • 2025: 156.8 million tickets (−13.6%); French films 37.7%, American films 35.8%.
  • Cinemas everywhere: from multiplexes to small cinémas d'art et d'essai (independent cinemas showing arthouse films).
  • Cannes each May: the world's best-known film festival.
  • la fréquentation – attendance · les entrées (f) – tickets sold, admissions · une salle (de cinéma) – a cinema, a screen · un(e) cinéphile – a film lover
  • en version originale (VO) – in the original language · en version française (VF) – dubbed into French (doublé) · sous-titré – subtitled
Quick check
?Hier soir, j'ai assisté à l'avant-première du film. What does this mean?
Mission 3

How France funds its cinema

  • L'exception culturelle: the idea that films are culture, not just goods, so the state may protect them (defended by France in world trade talks in 1993).
  • A tax on every cinema ticket goes to the CNC, which reinvests it in French films and cinemas.
  • L'avance sur recettes (since 1959): CNC loans for films chosen for their quality, often first films.
  • TV channels, and since 2021 streaming platforms, must invest part of their revenue in French and European works.
  • La chronologie des médias: rules on how long a film waits after its cinema release before it can be shown on pay TV, streaming, then free TV.
  • financer – to fund · une subvention – a subsidy · un producteur / une productrice · la sortie en salle – cinema release
Mission 3

Cinema in young people's lives

  • Competition: streaming platforms, series, short videos, games.
  • Why young people still go: a social outing, big releases on the big screen, special events (premieres, festivals).
  • What holds them back: ticket prices, films available soon on platforms.
  • Help: discount prices for young people; the pass Culture (a state credit for young people) can be spent on cinema tickets.
  • School screenings: many pupils discover French films through school programmes.
  • une plateforme de streaming · une série · une sortie – an outing; a release · le prix des places – ticket prices
Mission 3

Argue both sides

  • Do cinemas have a future?
  • Yes (arguments supporters make):
  • Voir un film en salle reste une expérience collective unique. – Seeing a film in a cinema remains a unique shared experience.
  • Les grands films sortent d'abord au cinéma. – Major films are released in cinemas first.
  • No, or not as before (arguments supporters make):
  • Les plateformes offrent un choix immense pour le prix d'une place. – Platforms offer a huge choice for the price of one ticket.
  • Le prix des places décourage les familles et les jeunes. – Ticket prices put off families and young people.
  • And state funding? Supporters: it keeps French and arthouse films alive. Critics: it funds films few people see.
  • Your turn: "Although streaming is convenient, nothing replaces the big screen."
    Show answer

    Bien que le streaming soit pratique, rien ne remplace le grand écran.

Quick check
?En 2025, la fréquentation des salles a baissé de 13,6 %. What does this mean?
Mission 3

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • le septième art · un réalisateur / une réalisatrice · un(e) cinéaste · le tournage · un long-métrage · la fréquentation · les entrées · une avant-première · en VO / doublé / sous-titré · l'exception culturelle · une subvention · la sortie en salle
  • Ce qui distingue la Nouvelle Vague, c'est sa liberté : tournage en extérieur, caméra légère et jeunes acteurs.
  • Bien que la fréquentation ait baissé en 2025, la France reste le premier marché du cinéma en Europe. (bien que + perfect subjunctive)
  • Si le CNC ne finançait pas les premiers films, beaucoup de jeunes réalisateurs ne pourraient pas tourner. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • Component 1 card (5 min preparation, 5–6 min): Media, art, film and music; film in the lives of young people.
Mission check

?Which statement about French cinema is accurate?

Link history (dates, the Nouvelle Vague) to today (figures, funding, streaming). Examiners reward that "then and now" range.

Mission 4

Mission 4: In France you may mock a religion but not insult its believers. Where exactly is the line?

Make a guess: In France you may mock a religion but not insult its believers. Where exactly is the line?

Mission 4

A freedom written into law

  • 1789, Declaration of the Rights of Man, article 11: « La libre communication des pensées et des opinions est un des droits les plus précieux de l'Homme. »
  • Law of 29 July 1881 on the freedom of the press: still the core text today.
  • Freedom has limits set by law:
  • la diffamation – defamation (a factual claim that damages a person's honour or reputation);
  • l'injure – insult;
  • la provocation à la haine – incitement to hatred or violence (e.g. on grounds of origin or religion);
  • l'apologie du terrorisme – glorifying terrorism.
  • Blasphemy is not an offence. You may mock or criticise a religion; you may not insult or incite hatred against people for their faith.
  • Watch out: la liberté d'expression – freedom of expression; la liberté de la presse – press freedom.
Quick check
?A French cartoonist publishes a drawing that mocks a religion's beliefs. No individual is targeted and there is no call to hatred. Under French law, what is the position?
Mission 4

When cartoons cost lives

  • Charlie Hebdo: a satirical weekly that had published caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad.
  • 7 January 2015: two gunmen attack its Paris office: 12 people killed, including cartoonists and two police officers.
  • 11 January 2015: about 4 million people march across France. Slogan: Je suis Charlie.
  • 16 October 2020: Samuel Paty, a history teacher, is murdered after showing caricatures in a lesson on freedom of expression.
  • The debate after these attacks (violence is condemned on all sides):
  • some defend an unconditional droit à la caricature – right to caricature;
  • others call for restraint out of respect for believers' feelings.
  • Watch out: un dessinateur – a cartoonist; un dessin de presse – a press cartoon.
Mission 4

The press: print, online, public

  • National dailies (les quotidiens nationaux): Le Monde, Le Figaro, Libération, Les Échos, L'Équipe (sport).
  • Regional press is strong: Ouest-France is the French daily with the biggest circulation.
  • Print sales fall; papers rely on digital subscriptions (les abonnements numériques) and paywalls.
  • Public broadcasting: France Télévisions, Radio France. The TV licence fee (la redevance) was abolished in 2022; funding now comes from a share of VAT revenue.
  • Francophone media: TV5Monde, RFI (Radio France Internationale), Le Devoir (Québec), Le Soir (Belgium).
  • Your turn: "Fewer and fewer young people read a printed newspaper."
    Show answer

    De moins en moins de jeunes lisent un journal papier.

Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "Sales of daily newspapers are falling."
Mission 4

Online: speed, falsehoods, rules

  • Most young people get news from social media (les réseaux sociaux), often through video.
  • Risks: les infox / les fake news – false news; la désinformation; le cyberharcèlement – online harassment; les bulles de filtre – filter bubbles.
  • 2018 law against the manipulation of information: in the three months before a national election, a judge, ruling within 48 hours, can order the spread of false news online to be stopped.
  • Arcom (since 2022): the regulator for broadcasting and online content.
  • EU Digital Services Act (fully in force 2024): platforms must remove illegal content and explain how their algorithms work.
  • Watch out: vérifier ses sources – to check your sources; un(e) internaute – an internet user.
Mission 4

Media, society and politics

  • Reporters sans frontières (RSF) 2026 index: France 25th of 180 countries.
  • RSF's concerns for France: ownership concentrated in a few large groups; protection of journalists' sources; unstable funding for public media.
  • Debate on ownership: business owners such as the Bolloré group (CNews, Europe 1, Le JDD) own several media.
  • Supporters say private investment keeps titles alive; critics fear owners influence editorial lines.
  • The C8 case: Arcom did not renew the TV channel's free-to-air licence; C8 stopped broadcasting on the TNT on 28 February 2025.
  • Arcom cited repeated breaches of its obligations (it had been fined several times); the Conseil d'État upheld the decision.
  • Supporters: a regulator applying the rules. Critics, including the channel's presenters: a blow to pluralism.
Quick check
?L'Arcom n'a pas renouvelé l'autorisation de diffusion de C8 sur la TNT. What does this mean?
Mission 4

Faut-il limiter la liberté d'expression ? Argue both sides

  • For firmer limits (arguments supporters make):
  • Les mots peuvent blesser et pousser à la violence, surtout sur les réseaux sociaux. – Words can hurt and lead to violence, especially on social media.
  • Les plateformes devraient retirer plus vite les contenus haineux. – Platforms should remove hateful content faster.
  • Against new limits (arguments supporters make):
  • Ce qui choque les uns doit pouvoir être dit, sinon c'est la censure. – What shocks some people must be sayable, or it is censorship.
  • Qui décidera de ce qui est vrai ? Ni l'État ni les plateformes ne devraient jouer ce rôle. – Who will decide what is true? Neither the state nor platforms should play that role.
  • Linkers: D'un côté … de l'autre … · Certes …, mais … · Il n'en reste pas moins que …
  • Your turn: "It is true that satire shocks, but it is essential in a democracy."
    Show answer

    Certes, la satire choque, mais elle est essentielle en démocratie.

Mission 4

Vocabulary bank and model sentences

  • la liberté d'expression · la censure · l'autocensure – self-censorship · un(e) journaliste · la presse écrite · un quotidien / un hebdomadaire – a daily / a weekly · un abonnement · une source · une infox · le pluralisme · un média indépendant · diffuser – to broadcast · la ligne éditoriale
  • Il faut que les journalistes puissent enquêter sans pression. (il faut que + subjunctive)
  • Bien que la presse papier soit en déclin, les médias en ligne n'ont jamais eu autant de lecteurs. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • Si les jeunes vérifiaient leurs sources, les infox se propageraient moins vite. (si + imperfect → conditional)

  • Component 1 card (5 min preparation, 5–6 min): trends in media; how young people get their news.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Parisian artists once called the Eiffel Tower useless and monstrous. Who decides what great art is?

Make a guess: Parisian artists once called the Eiffel Tower useless and monstrous. Who decides what great art is?

Mission 5

Three buildings, three scandals

  • Eiffel Tower (1889), built for the World's Fair, a century after the Revolution.
  • In 1887 leading artists and writers protested in the press against « l'inutile et monstrueuse tour Eiffel ». It was meant to last 20 years.
  • Centre Pompidou (1977), by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers: pipes and escalators on the outside. Closed for renovation in 2025; reopening planned for 2030.
  • Louvre Pyramid (1989), by I. M. Pei: glass and steel in a royal palace courtyard. Many called it an insult to heritage.
  • All three are now icons of Paris.
  • Watch out: un monument – a landmark; un bâtiment – a building; un édifice – an (imposing) building.
Mission 5

Notre-Dame: rebuild as before, or modernise?

  • 15 April 2019: fire destroys the roof and the 19th-century spire of Notre-Dame de Paris.
  • Debate: rebuild identically, or add a contemporary touch (a modern spire was suggested)?
  • Decision: the spire was rebuilt as it was (Viollet-le-Duc's design).
  • Work was largely funded by private donations.
  • 7 December 2024: the cathedral reopens, five years after the fire.
  • Your turn: "The spire was rebuilt identically."
    Show answer

    La flèche a été reconstruite à l'identique. (passive: être + past participle agreeing with la flèche)

Quick check
?Notre-Dame a rouvert ses portes en décembre 2024, cinq ans après l'incendie. What does this mean?
Mission 5

Painting: from scandal to blockbuster

  • 1874: a group refused by the official Salon holds its own exhibition. Monet shows Impression, soleil levant (1872).
  • A critic mocks them as « impressionnistes ». The name sticks.
  • Their aim: capture light and the moment, painted quickly, often outdoors.
  • Today the Musée d'Orsay (a former railway station, museum since 1986) holds the largest Impressionist collection.
  • 20th century: Paris is a hub for Cubism (Picasso, Braque) and later for street art.
  • French-speaking Africa: Dak'Art, the Dakar Biennale of contemporary African art, held since the early 1990s.
  • Model: Ce tableau, jugé scandaleux à l'époque, est aujourd'hui considéré comme un chef-d'œuvre.
Mission 5

Literature: guardians, prizes, new voices

  • L'Académie française (1635): 40 members (les Immortels) who write the official dictionary. First woman elected: Marguerite Yourcenar, 1980.
  • Le prix Goncourt (first awarded 1903): the top French novel prize; the cheque is only €10, but sales soar.
  • Annie Ernaux: Nobel Prize in Literature, 2022, the first French woman to win it.
  • French-speaking voices:
  • Léopold Sédar Senghor (Senegal) and Aimé Césaire (Martinique): la négritude, a movement affirming Black identity and culture;
  • Maryse Condé (Guadeloupe);
  • Leïla Slimani (Goncourt 2016) and Mohamed Mbougar Sarr (Senegal, Goncourt 2021).
  • Watch out: un roman – a novel; un(e) romancier/romancière – a novelist; une œuvre – a work.
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "The Goncourt has been awarded since 1903."
Mission 5

Who pays, and who gets in?

  • 1959: first Ministry of Culture, with the writer André Malraux as minister. Aim: make great works accessible to as many people as possible.
  • Le 1 % artistique (since 1951): about 1% of the cost of many public buildings pays for a work of art.
  • National museums are free for under-26s living in the EU.
  • Le pass Culture: credit for young people (€150 at 18 since 2025) to spend on books, concerts, cinema.
  • The Louvre, about 9 million visitors a year, is the world's most visited museum. The theft of Crown jewels in October 2025 raised questions about security and funding.
  • Representation: who is shown in museums and prizes? Critics note few women and artists from minorities in collections; museums now buy and show more of their work.
Mission 5

L'État doit-il financer la culture ? Argue both sides

  • Yes, public funding (arguments supporters make):
  • La culture ne doit pas être réservée à ceux qui peuvent payer. – Culture must not be only for those who can pay.
  • Le patrimoine attire des millions de touristes : c'est un investissement. – Heritage draws millions of tourists: it is an investment.
  • Less public funding (arguments supporters make):
  • En temps de crise, l'argent public devrait aller d'abord à la santé et à l'école. – In hard times, public money should go first to health and schools.
  • Le mécénat privé peut financer la culture, comme pour Notre-Dame. – Private patronage can fund culture, as with Notre-Dame.
  • Linkers: Il est indéniable que … · En revanche, … · À mon sens, …
  • Your turn: "Museums should be free for everyone."
    Show answer

    Les musées devraient être gratuits pour tout le monde.

Mission 5

Talking about a work of art

  • Describe: Au premier plan – in the foreground · à l'arrière-plan – in the background · au centre · à gauche / à droite.
  • Analyse: L'artiste met en lumière … – highlights · L'œuvre dénonce … – denounces · Les couleurs vives évoquent … – bright colours evoke.
  • Judge: Ce qui me frappe, c'est … – What strikes me is … · À mon avis, l'œuvre a pour but de …
  • Model (our own description of Monet's Impression, soleil levant, the earlier screen): Au premier plan, deux petites barques glissent sur l'eau. À l'arrière-plan, on devine un port dans la brume. Les touches rapides évoquent le mouvement de l'eau. Ce qui me frappe, c'est que le soleil, petit et orange, attire immédiatement le regard.
  • Watch out: une toile – a canvas/painting; une peinture – a painting or paint; un tableau – a painting (the most common word).
Quick check
?In a description of a painting, what does à l'arrière-plan mean?
Mission 5

Vocabulary bank and exam tasks

  • un(e) artiste · un chef-d'œuvre · une exposition · un musée / une galerie · le patrimoine · un(e) architecte · restaurer · à l'identique · un prix littéraire · décerner – to award · le mécénat – patronage · l'accès à la culture
  • Component 1 card (5 min preparation, 5–6 min): trends in art, or museums and galleries.
Mission check

?Which statement is accurate?

Name a work, a date and a debate, then give your view. That is what examiners reward on this topic.

Mission 6

Mission 6: French is spoken on five continents. Why, and what did the colonial past leave behind?

Make a guess: French is spoken on five continents. Why, and what did the colonial past leave behind?

Mission 6

The French-speaking world

  • About 396 million French speakers worldwide (OIF report, 2026), which ranks French as the world's fourth most spoken language.
  • About two thirds of them live in Africa.
  • French is an official language in 32 states and governments, e.g. Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Canada (with Québec), Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti.
  • la francophonie (small f) = all French speakers and places.
  • la Francophonie (capital F) = the institutions, above all the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF).
  • The word was coined by the geographer Onésime Reclus around 1880.
  • un(e) francophone · un pays francophone · la langue officielle · la langue maternelle
Mission 6

Why there? Two colonial empires

  • First empire (17th–18th centuries):
  • 1608: Champlain founds Québec (New France);
  • West Indies: Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint-Domingue (today Haiti), economies built on slavery;
  • 1763: France loses most of New France to Britain.
  • Haiti wins independence in 1804 after a slave revolt.
  • Slavery in the French colonies: abolished 1794, restored 1802, abolished for good on 27 April 1848 (Victor Schœlcher).
  • Second empire (19th–20th centuries):
  • Algeria from 1830; West and Central Africa, Madagascar, Indochina; protectorates in Tunisia (1881) and Morocco (1912).
  • Belgium ruled the Congo, Rwanda and Burundi: one reason why the DR Congo is today the largest French-speaking country by population.
  • Not every French-speaking place is a former colony: Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Monaco are not.
Quick check
?Le Sénégal est membre de la Francophonie. What does the capital F tell you?
Mission 6

Decolonisation, 1945–1962

  • 8 May 1945, Sétif (Algeria): demonstrations, then violent repression; thousands of Algerians killed (figures disputed).
  • 1946–1954: war in Indochina; defeat at Diên Biên Phu (7 May 1954); the Geneva Accords end French rule in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.
  • 1956: Morocco and Tunisia independent.
  • 1960: 14 territories under French rule in sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar become independent, e.g. Senegal, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon.
  • 1954–1962: Algerian War:
  • Évian Accords (18 March 1962); independence on 5 July 1962;
  • hundreds of thousands of French settlers (les pieds-noirs) leave for France;
  • many harkis (Algerians who served in the French army) are left behind, and many killed.
  • la décolonisation · l'indépendance · un colon – settler · la guerre d'Algérie
Mission 6

Who stayed French?

  • 1946: Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana and Réunion become départements (law championed by Aimé Césaire, poet and deputy for Martinique).
  • Mayotte became a département in 2011.
  • Today: five DROM (overseas departments and regions) and several overseas collectivities, e.g. French Polynesia.
  • New Caledonia: three referendums (2018, 2020, 2021) rejected independence; pro-independence parties boycotted the third. Serious unrest in 2024; an agreement on a new status (Bougival, July 2025) has not been put into the Constitution, and the question remains open.
  • Creole languages (e.g. in Guadeloupe, Martinique, Réunion, Haiti): most words come from French; the grammar is their own, shaped by African and other languages.
  • l'outre-mer · un territoire ultramarin · le créole · l'identité
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "If France had granted independence earlier, the war could have been avoided."
Mission 6

The OIF

  • 20 March 1970, Niamey (Niger): founding of the agency that became the OIF; founders include Léopold Sédar Senghor (Senegal), Habib Bourguiba (Tunisia), Hamani Diori (Niger) and Norodom Sihanouk (Cambodia).
  • 20 March is the Journée internationale de la Francophonie.
  • 90 states and governments (2026): 53 members, 5 associate members, 32 observers. Some members are not French-speaking countries.
  • Secretary General: Louise Mushikiwabo (Rwanda), since 2019.
  • Aims: the French language, cultural diversity, education, democracy and human rights.
  • 2025: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, ruled by military governments, left the OIF, calling it a political tool.
  • Summits: 2024 in France (Villers-Cotterêts and Paris); November 2026 in Phnom Penh (Cambodia), where members postponed the choice of the next Secretary General by a year.
Mission 6

Colonial legacies today

  • Language: French remains an official or widely used language in many former colonies; Rwanda moved its schools to English in 2008.
  • Money: the CFA franc is still used in 14 African countries; a 2019 reform ended the obligation for West African states to keep half their reserves in France.
  • Military: between 2022 and 2025 French troops left Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Chad and Senegal.
  • Memory:
  • 2001: a French law recognises the slave trade and slavery as a crime against humanity (loi Taubira);
  • 2005: a law asks schools to teach the "positive role" of the French presence overseas; after protests, that line is removed in 2006;
  • 2021: reports on Algeria (Benjamin Stora) and on Rwanda (Vincent Duclert);
  • 2021: France returns 26 royal treasures of Abomey to Benin.
Mission 6

Argue both sides

  • Should France apologise for colonisation?
  • Arguments supporters make: Reconnaître les crimes du passé permet d'apaiser les mémoires. – Recognising past crimes helps heal memories.
  • Arguments opponents make: On ne peut pas juger le passé avec les valeurs d'aujourd'hui ; il faut plutôt que les historiens travaillent. – We cannot judge the past by today's values; historians should do the work.
  • Is the Francophonie a shared space or a tool of influence?
  • La Francophonie permet à des pays très différents de défendre ensemble la diversité culturelle. – It lets very different countries defend cultural diversity together.
  • Pour certains, la Francophonie sert surtout l'influence de la France. – For some, it mainly serves France's influence.
  • Linkers: Selon ses partisans … · Ses détracteurs estiment que … · Tout dépend de …
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "Algeria, whose independence was proclaimed in 1962, …"
Mission 6

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • la francophonie · un empire colonial · la colonisation · la décolonisation · l'esclavage – slavery · l'indépendance · l'outre-mer · le métissage – mixing of cultures · l'héritage – legacy · le devoir de mémoire – duty to remember · la repentance · la restitution · le rayonnement – influence, prestige
  • Le français, qui était la langue du colonisateur, est devenu une langue partagée par des millions d'Africains.
  • Bien que la colonisation soit terminée, ses conséquences se font encore sentir. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • Ce qui compte pour beaucoup d'Africains, c'est moins le passé que l'avenir de leur langue. (cleft)
  • Component 1 card (5 min preparation, 5–6 min): regional culture and heritage in a French-speaking country (e.g. Martinique, Québec).
Mission check

?Which sentence is accurate?

Back facts with dates and named examples (1848, 1960, 1962, 1970, 2021), and present each view on the colonial past as the view of its supporters.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Le patrimoine: national / regional / local; material / intangible (baguette 2022, repas gastronomique 2010); 56 UNESCO sites.
  • Protection: the state, Journées du patrimoine (1984), Loto du patrimoine (2018), volunteers; tourism (102 million visitors in 2025) helps and harms.
  • Regional languages: heritage (art. 75-1) but French is the language of the Republic (art. 2); 2021 immersion ruling.

Mission 2

  • Diversity: France, Belgium, Québec, the Caribbean, West and Central Africa; many languages mixed with French.
  • Change: chanson → yé-yé → rap → French touch → streaming era (rap dominant; 16 of the top 20 albums of 2025 French).
  • Safeguarding: radio quotas (1994: 40% in French), CNM (2020), festivals, Fête de la musique (1982).

Mission 3

  • Le septième art: Canudo's name for cinema, which combines the other six arts; first paid screening, Paris, 1895.
  • Stages: Méliès (1902) → Renoir → CNC and Cannes (1946) → Nouvelle Vague (1959–60s) → Césars (1976) → popular comedies → streaming.
  • Passion and protection: 181.5 m tickets (2024), 156.8 m (2025); exception culturelle, ticket tax, CNC.

Mission 4

  • Freedom of expression: 1789 (art. 11), law of 29 July 1881; limits: defamation, insult, incitement to hatred, glorifying terrorism; blasphemy is not an offence.
  • 2015 Charlie Hebdo, 2020 Samuel Paty; online rules: 2018 law, Arcom (2022), EU DSA.
  • RSF 2026: France 25th of 180; debates on ownership and the C8 decision (2025).

Mission 5

  • Eiffel Tower (1889), Pompidou (1977), Pyramid (1989): scandals that became icons; Notre-Dame burned 2019, reopened 2024, rebuilt identically.
  • Impressionism (1874); Académie française (1635); Goncourt (1903); Ernaux Nobel 2022; négritude; Slimani, Sarr.
  • Funding and access: Ministry of Culture (1959), 1 % artistique, free museums for under-26s, pass Culture.

Mission 6

  • About 396 million French speakers, two thirds in Africa; francophonie (people) vs Francophonie (OIF, 90 states and governments).
  • Two empires → decolonisation (Indochina 1954, Africa 1960, Algeria 1962) → overseas départements since 1946.
  • Legacies: language, CFA franc, troops withdrawn 2022–25, memory laws (2001, 2005), reports and restitutions (2021).
